_about: Flame Atlas prepared answers (Team Flame Atlas, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026). Answers to the questions the dashboard's buttons ask, written in advance with an AI assistant (Claude) from the team's curated NASA documents and tests table, and checked against the cited source pages in a second AI pass; same format as the live chat's answers. Every point names its source and page.

answers.question: Why did test BASS:1 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22.1% O2) burn?

data.text: A 2 cm wide SIBAL fabric strip burned in microgravity in the ISS glovebox at 22.1% O2 and 98.29 kPa, in concurrent flow logged at 10 then 5 cm/s, with a pre-wired igniter; the log records extinction at burnout near the sample end.

In BAS-05, a 2.2 cm SIBAL sample on the ISS at 21% O2 in concurrent flow burned to complete burnout in about 40 s at 10 cm/s; at 5 cm/s the flame was shorter, spread more slowly and took more than 60 s.
The 2012 BASS slides show a 2 cm sample in concurrent flow ignited at 10 cm/s, the flow then reduced to 5 cm/s; the deck prints no test number, and the team matches the video to this test.

inferred.text: This test's 22.1% O2 is above the whole oxygen range of the quenching boundary BAS-05 draws for 2.2 cm SIBAL in concurrent flow, about 16.8 to 18.9% O2 at about 2.2 to 3.7 cm/s (read from a figure), and its 5 cm/s flow is above those speeds.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: BASS:1 (2 cm SIBAL, microgravity, 22.1% O2, concurrent flow cut from 10 to 5 cm/s) burned until burnout near the sample end, as the log records.

answer.not_covered: No document gives a spread rate or burn time tied to this test.

answers.question: Why did test BASS:10 (PMMA, 21.9% O2) go out?

data.text: A 1 cm PMMA sphere burned in microgravity on the ISS at 21.89% O2 and 100.33 kPa and went out with the flow logged as 'fan off' (0 cm/s).
The BASS deck reports a PMMA sample of 15-mm initial diameter, at a nominal 17% O2, 101.3 kPa and under 1 cm/s, whose flame survived a nitrogen jet and went out at zero flow.
The same sphere's last run, BASS:11, at the same 21.89% O2 and 100.33 kPa (flow logged as 'at 42', no unit), burned until its fuel ran out and is labelled burned.

BAS-01 Appendix D reports that sample 19, a 1-cm PMMA sphere of initial mass 617.5 mg, was completely consumed in four tests; its Table D.2 gives test 20, this run by test number (the team's match), a burn of 1 min 15 s.

inferred.text: This flame went out at 21.89% O2, above the nominal 17% O2 at which the BASS deck shows PMMA spheres burning in flow; the logged fan turn-off, not the oxygen level, is what coincides with the extinction.

other_side.note: the same sphere's last run burned until its fuel ran out

lead.text: BASS:10 (1 cm PMMA sphere, 21.89% O2, microgravity) went out with the fan logged off; the sphere's last run burned until its fuel ran out (BASS:11).

answer.not_covered: No document explains why these flames went out when the flow stopped.

answers.question: Why did test BASS:101 (Paraffin wax, 16.1% O2) not ignite?

data.text: A paraffin wax candle (sample 44) on the ISS in microgravity at 16.05% O2 and 99.5 kPa, with air display cells 5 and 10 (no unit printed), did not ignite despite prolonged attempted ignition; no pictures were taken.
The log's only comment on the cause is a question: 'Candle out of wax?'.

Just before, the same candle at 16.05% O2 and 99.5 kPa ignited in what the log calls "'concurrent' or stagnation" flow and kept a flame through fan pot settings 0.5 down to 0.32, then went out at 14:22:50.

other_side.note: the same candle ignited in the run just before

lead.text: This paraffin candle did not ignite in microgravity at 16.05% O2 despite prolonged attempts; the log only asks 'Candle out of wax?', and the same candle had lit just before.

answer.not_covered: The log lists this run among test points without data files (sheet 'TP without Data').

answers.question: Why did test BASS:102 (Japan wax, 16.3% O2) burn?

data.text: A Japan wax candle (sample 40) burned in microgravity on the ISS at 16.3% O2 and 99.5 kPa, air display '5,3, 2, etc', fan pots '1.5, 1 0.5, 0.4'; the flame went out when, per the log, the candle was out of wax.
The log describes a nice blue flame with inner soot until low flows; at extinction the stagnation zone opened up before the flame went out, which the log marks '(out of wax)'.
BASS:89_87, an earlier run of the same candle at 15.9% O2 and 98.29 kPa with the flow logged at 2 cm/s (direction not logged), went out at a flow change.

other_side.note: the same candle at a slightly lower O2 went out at a flow change

lead.text: BASS:102 (Japan wax candle, microgravity, 16.3% O2) burned until its wax ran out, per the log; the same candle's earlier BASS:89_87, at 15.9% O2, went out at a flow change.

answer.not_covered: The log gives no flow speed in cm/s at extinction for this run.

answers.question: Why did test BASS:103 (Paraffin wax, 16.3% O2) go out?

data.text: A new paraffin wax slab (sample 42) on the ISS in microgravity at 16.3% O2 and 99.5 kPa held a blue flame around its leading edge that never spread; it went out on its own after 75 s, at flow setting 0.4 (no unit).

Every run logged as a paraffin slab went out: in BASS:78, at 21.93% O2, 98.55 kPa and 3 cm/s, the flame shrank and went out by itself; in BASS:79, at 21.93% and 6 cm/s, it went out when the igniter was retracted (directions not logged).
The BASS 2013 deck's operation steps caption flame extinction generally as 'Flow reduced too far or fuel consumed', without naming a test or material.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents: every run logged as a paraffin slab went out

answers.question: Why did test BASS:104 (PMMA, 17.2% O2) burn?

data.text: BASS:104: a new 2-cm PMMA sphere, sample 26, on the ISS in microgravity at 17.2% O2, 98.99 kPa and 5 cm/s. It took 4 min of tries and brief flames to ignite, then grew to wrap past 90 degrees: a short burn, about 2 min.

The BASS deck's summary reports flames at about 1 to 5 cm/s growing stronger and more luminous with time, which the authors attribute to the flame continually heating the solid and raising its vaporization rate.
On the same sphere at 17.24% O2 and 99.3 kPa, BASS:110 went out when the fan pot was turned down to 0.29.

other_side.note: the same sphere at 17.24% O2 went out when the fan was turned down

lead.text: BASS:104, a 2-cm PMMA sphere at 17.2% O2 and 5 cm/s in microgravity, burned about 2 min; at 17.24% O2 the same sphere went out at fan pot 0.29 (BASS:110).

answer.not_covered: The log does not say how this burn ended.

answers.question: Why did test BASS:110 (PMMA, 17.2% O2) go out?

data.text: BASS:110: the 2-cm sphere (sample 26, logged as PMMA on its first run) on the ISS in microgravity at 17.24% O2 and 99.3 kPa. At "near limit flow" the flame shrank forward and oscillated slightly at fan pot 0.35, then went out at pot 0.29.

In BASS-II tests of PMMA rods in axial stagnation (concurrent) flow on the ISS, the report finds quenching at very low forced flows: the flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue flame and oscillates with increasing amplitude just before going out.
Earlier that day, at 17.17% O2 and 99.3 kPa, the same sphere kept an all-blue flame below 1 cm/s in BASS:108.

inferred.text: This sphere's logged sequence, a flame that shrank forward and oscillated slightly before going out at a lower fan setting, resembles the quenching the BASS-II report describes for PMMA rods; no document makes this comparison.

other_side.note: the same sphere at 17.17% O2 kept burning below 1 cm/s

lead.text: BASS:110's flame (2-cm PMMA sphere, 17.24% O2, microgravity) shrank, oscillated slightly and went out at fan pot 0.29; at 17.17% O2, BASS:108 kept burning below 1 cm/s.

answer.not_covered: No airflow speed is logged for fan pot 0.29.

answers.question: Why did test BASS:12 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 21.6% O2) burn?

data.text: A 2 cm SIBAL strip burned in microgravity in the BASS duct at 21.63% O2 and 99.67 kPa in 22 cm/s concurrent flow, pre-wired igniter; the log gives a 26 s burn.
SAF-06 lists this test (by the team's match; 2.2 by 10 cm sample) at 21.6% O2 and 101 kPa, where the log has 99.67 kPa: spread 0.51 cm/s, flame length 6.2 cm, long and sooty.

The authors' core-flow estimate, which they say seems to explain the spread trends across duct sizes, gives the 2.2 cm BASS test in the smallest duct the most flow acceleration; it also had the paper's fastest spread, although its flame was much smaller.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

answers.question: Why did test BASS:14 (Nomex HT90-40, 21.6% O2) not ignite?

data.text: A strip logged 'Nomex blend 2 cm' (Nomex HT90-40 by the team's reading), on the ISS in microgravity at 21.63% O2, 99.67 kPa and 15 cm/s, ignited briefly, no sustained flame: it burned about 2 s and died when the igniter was turned off.

The 2013 BASS slides report that Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 samples did not burn in the ISS atmosphere at 21 to 22% O2 and flows around 15 cm/s; the authors note this is similar to 1 g, with narrower samples on the ISS.
The log adds that repeated re-ignition attempts failed and that the crew member felt the igniter should have been left on longer.

In OVR-03's drop-tower tests of Nomex HT90-40 (0 g, 30 cm/s concurrent flow, 101.35 kPa, flame lit in 1 g in enriched O2), the lowest O2 that burned the whole test (0-g ULOI) was 23% and the highest at which the flame went out (0-g MOC) 22%.

inferred.text: This test's 21.63% O2 is below both 0-g limits OVR-03 gives for this fabric (MOC 22%, ULOI 23%, at 30 cm/s concurrent flow), though those drop-tower flames were lit in enriched O2 and lasted about 5 s.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: BASS:14 (Nomex HT90-40 by the team's reading, microgravity, 21.63% O2) burned about 2 s, dying when the igniter was turned off; BAS-03 reports these samples did not burn.

answer.not_covered: The log gives no flow direction for this test.

data.text: A 'PMMA 2 cm' sample burned in microgravity on the ISS at 21.7% O2, 99.7 kPa and 11 cm/s (air display, no unit printed); a nitrogen jet (pot 8, then 10) did not extinguish it, and it went out.
The log records the fan was accidentally turned up briefly, then turned to 40 (no unit) at 16:19:22, and the flame out at 16:19:34 (all times GBX).
At nearly the same atmosphere, 21.75% O2 and 98.9 kPa, a 2 cm PMMA sphere burned about 4.75 minutes (BASS:33, flow logged as 6, 4, 9, no unit); its ending is not stated.

The BASS deck reports that extinction with the nitrogen jet was not possible at the given flow rate (rate not printed); the authors give this as one result of thicker solids storing a great deal of heat even with only a small flame.

inferred.text: This flame went out at 21.7% O2, above the nominal 17% O2 at which the BASS deck shows PMMA spheres burning in flow; the logged fan change, not the oxygen level, is what coincides with the extinction.

other_side.note: a 2 cm PMMA sphere burned at nearly the same atmosphere

lead.text: BASS:15 ('PMMA 2 cm' sample, 21.7% O2, microgravity) went out after the fan was turned to 40, the log shows; a 2 cm PMMA sphere burned at 21.75% O2 (BASS:33).

answer.not_covered: The log prints no unit for the fan setting of 40.

The author separates steady from self-extinguished flames by a computed flame temperature of 1100–1200 K (1100 K alone in Chapter 4), extinction cases computed below it, never steady; Fig. 5.2 also shows some self-extinguished flames computed above that band and some fuel-terminated ones below it.
Test BRE:20352D2, also an ethylene-nitrogen test on the 25 mm burner in still air in microgravity, burned at 34.04% O2 and 104 kPa.
In Fig. 6.1 the self-extinguished flames stood at about 0.5 to 0.9 of their computed steady flame length; the author takes this to mean they were relatively far from steady when they went out.

inferred.text: Tests of this fuel family on this burner at nearly the same oxygen and pressure ended both ways, so oxygen and pressure alone do not settle the outcome here; the thesis reports that lower fuel heats of combustion and higher oxygen help flames burn longer (round 1).

answers.question: Why did test FLARE:RUN#01 (Filter paper, 14.3% O2) go out?

data.text: 0.12 mm filter paper, 40 mm wide, microgravity (ISS/Kibo SCEM), 100 kPa, 14.3% O2 and 6 cm/s opposed flow, Kanthal hot wire on from T + 5 s for 10 s: the flame went out immediately after ignition.

The pre-flight model expected a minimum limiting oxygen of 14.0% at 8 cm/s opposed flow and a much wider flammable range below 10 cm/s; the authors write that, contrary to these predictions, this run's flame went out immediately.

Below 10 cm/s opposed flow the measured limiting oxygen was higher than the pre-flight curve; the authors attribute this to the sample's boundary layer, where preheat length varies inversely with the square root of opposed flow.

answers.question: Why did test OVR-03:nodate:KIMWIPES-FIG9-CON30:227dd5be (Kimwipes tissue paper, 40% O2) burn?

data.text: Kimwipes tissue (thin cellulose), 5 × 10 cm, microgravity drop-tower rig, about 40% O2 in a normoxic atmosphere, 30 cm/s concurrent flow, hot wire lit at release: burned, spreading at about 26 mm/s (read from a figure).

The authors tested Kimwipes, thin cellulose that chars as it burns and is not treated for fire resistance, to expand the thin-cellulose database; with it they can obtain spread and extinction data in the short drop time.
Along the normoxic curve, the report's correlations predict opposed spread rising quickly with O2 and concurrent spread rising more slowly, as the falling pressure offsets the rising O2.
In this Fig. 9 series (microgravity, 30 cm/s concurrent flow), spread went from about 22 mm/s at about 24% O2 to about 31 mm/s at about 85% (read from the figure).

The authors tested Kimwipes, thin cellulose that chars as it burns and is not treated for fire resistance, to expand the thin-cellulose database; with it they can obtain spread and extinction data in the short drop time.

answers.question: What does the burn limit OVR-03:nodate:NOMEXHT90-40-0G-MOC:af026ee4 (Nomex HT90-40, 22% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Microgravity limit (0g MOC) of Nomex HT90-40 fabric, 12 mil, in a drop-tower rig at 101.35 kPa, 30 cm/s concurrent flow: 22% O2, the highest oxygen at which the flame went out during the drop.
Each 5 × 10 cm sample was lit by a hot wire in 1 g, in oxygen above the 1g ULOI; the test gas reached it shortly after the 5.18 s drop began, leaving the flame about 5 s in it.

This is the report's own drop-tower result; a 2012 paper reprints the value as earlier data (same data: the team's reading). The authors call these limits a conservative measure of 0g limits, since some flames might go out given longer.
The Earth-gravity Test 1 MOC of the same fabric at 101.35 kPa, WSTF data the report cites, is also 22% O2 (Table 1); a 2012 paper prints 22.1%.

lead.text: Microgravity MOC of Nomex HT90-40 fabric at 101.35 kPa, 30 cm/s concurrent flow: 22% O2, the highest oxygen at which a drop-tower flame went out.

answers.question: What does the burn limit OVR-03:nodate:VITONA-1G-MOC:69d467ab (Viton A, 21% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Earth-gravity maximum oxygen concentration (1g MOC) of Viton A in the upward NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 at about 101.35 kPa: about 21% O2, read from the report's Fig. 10, which plots 1g MOC against total pressure.

The report defines the 1g MOC, citing the Test 1 standard, as the oxygen at which at least five samples passed, with at least one failure at 1% more O2. Fig. 10 plots cited WSTF data (its ref. 7), without sample form, thickness or igniter.
In the same Fig. 10 series, Viton A's 1g MOC reads about 21% O2 at about 85.5 kPa and about 29% at about 48.26 kPa.

The report says most Test 1 MOCs vary mainly with oxygen, not pressure, and the few exceptions appear to share halogens (the legend marks Viton A as containing them); it attributes this to halogens scavenging free radicals, which inhibits the flame's heat release; at low pressure more diffusive mixing increases scavenging, and the reduced heat release raises the oxygen limit.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Viton A's Earth-gravity Test 1 MOC, the highest oxygen at which samples consistently self-extinguish, at about 101.35 kPa: about 21% O2, cited WSTF data read from the report's Fig. 10.

answer.not_covered: No microgravity or partial-gravity test of Viton A in the documents.

data.text: Earth-gravity maximum oxygen concentration (1g MOC) of Zytel 42 in the upward NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 at about 48.26 kPa: about 25% O2, read from the report's Fig. 10, which plots 1g MOC against total pressure.

The report defines the 1g MOC, citing the Test 1 standard, as the oxygen at which at least five samples passed, with at least one failure at 1% more O2. Fig. 10 plots cited WSTF data (its ref. 7), without sample form, thickness or igniter.
In the same Fig. 10 series, Zytel 42's 1g MOC reads about 23% O2 at about 101.35 kPa and about 23% at about 85.5 kPa.

The report says WSTF's Test 1 MOCs generally vary mainly with oxygen, not pressure, which it finds somewhat surprising for an upward test; it proposes, as a hypothesis still to verify, that the upward limit is set essentially by the critical heat flux for ignition.

data.text: Martian-gravity MOC* of Nomex HT90-40, a 12 mil fabric, at 101.3 kPa with concurrent buoyant flow: 19% O2, the highest oxygen at which the flame was seen to self-extinguish within the drop time.
This paper's own tests, on a centrifuge in the NASA Glenn drop tower at 30.8 RPM (0.38 g at the igniter); a hot wire at the outer end of the 5 × 15 cm opening came on 2.1 s before the 5.18 s drop.

answers.question: What does the burn limit OVR-05:nodate:EPOXYGLASS-HALF-MOC-T9:b6249a5b (Epoxy/glass, 16% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) of epoxy/glass laminate (NEMA G-11, 0.064 in., 1.63 mm) as ½-in.-wide strips, 7 in. long, in 1-g upward tests at 101.35 kPa: 16% O2, where all samples (at least five) passed.

The report's own tests: oxygen in 1% steps (ASTM D 2863), closed 1400-L chamber, initially quiescent; strips held at the top, without the standard wing-nut fixture; Test 1 burn-length criterion; igniter not stated for Table 9.

Table 9: this laminate gave ULOI 17.9 and MOC 16% O2 as ½-in. strips, 23.6 and 23% O2 as standard-mounted 2.5-in. samples; the report finds all materials tested as ½-in. strips except PET film gave significantly lower thresholds.

The authors say flight-test restrictions, such as limited space in closed chambers, will prevent testing standard-size samples, so correlating rods and narrow samples with standard data was considered necessary; to minimize oxygen depletion in flight experiments they recommend 1/8-in. rods or ½-in. wide samples with 1- or 2-in. burn-length criteria.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: MOC of ½-in. epoxy/glass laminate strips in the report's 1-g upward tests at 101.35 kPa: 16% O2, where all samples passed, in 1% oxygen steps.

answers.question: What does the burn limit OVR-05:nodate:NBR-EDGE-MOC-T5:6734e10d (NBR, 16.1% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) of nitrile rubber (NBR) sheet, Rubberite, 0.063 in. (1.6 mm), one vertical edge exposed, in 1-g upward tests at 101.35 kPa: 16.1% O2, where all samples (at least five) passed.

The report's own tests: oxygen in 1% steps (ASTM D 2863), closed 1400-L chamber, initially quiescent; samples 7 in. long, held along the top and one side; chemical igniter below the bottom edge; Test 1 burn-length criterion.

For this nitrile, standard mounting gave ULOI 16.6 and MOC 16.1% O2, one exposed edge 16.5 and 16.1% O2; the report finds exposed edges mostly gave higher thresholds, though the difference was very small.

Citing another study, the report says an edge flame gets more oxygen and heats the sample more efficiently, which could give higher flame spread over exposed edges in microgravity. The authors add that near-extinction conditions may be controlled by other factors than those controlling spread rate under stable burning, and that extinguishment-controlling factors could differ between 1 g and microgravity.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

The interim standard NASA-STD-(I)-6001B defines the MOC as the highest oxygen concentration at which at least five specimens pass the Test 1 acceptance criteria; the presentation's own Test 1 slide says a sample burning more than 15 cm fails.

The Ferkul et al. 2026 LPSC presentation reproduces Table 2 from Tapia Harper, Juarez, Woods and Beeson's 2017 ICES paper on sample length impact on the Test 1 MOC; the values are that study's, not the presentation's own measurement. Table 2's footnote gives all O2 measurements a tolerance of +0.15%/−0.0%.
The same Table 2 row gives Solimide TA-301, 30 cm samples, an upward limiting oxygen index (ULOI) of 24.3, also without a unit.

inferred.text: Across the 18, 20 and 30 cm samples of Solimide TA-301, Table 2 gives MOC values of 23.0, 23.0 and 23.1, a spread of 0.1; this 30 cm value is the highest. Units not printed.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Solimide TA-301, 30-cm samples, 70.3 kPa, 1 g (team's reading): NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 maximum oxygen concentration 23.1 (no unit printed), reported by a 2017 sample-length study.

answers.question: What does the burn limit SOF-02:nodate:PMMA-FUNDAMENTALLIMIT:d2cfdf4b (PMMA, 14% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: The lowest O2 that sustains burning, called the fundamental limit after an earlier study: slightly below 14% O2, at the bottom of SOF-02's extinction boundary around 10 cm/s forced flow (strain rate 7.5 1/s); 4-cm PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity, 101.3 kPa (1 ± 0.05 atm).

It rests on SOF-02's 35-test map: O2 and flow read at the duct entrance at extinction (±0.25%), the intermediate-flow boundary found by O2 depletion. Open 'in-between' symbols lie at the extinction boundary's bottom: near 10 cm/s quenching was difficult to tell from blowoff on video.

This is SOF-02's own data. It says this and earlier rod data show the PMMA O2 limit can be below 14%, and calls that considerably lower than the normal-gravity PMMA LOI and upward-flammability values in conventional flammability tables.

The lowest in-between point reads about 13.55% O2 at about 11.5 cm/s. Fig. 8's lowest O2, about 13.3% at about 42.4 cm/s, is a total (wake) blowoff, whose limiting O2 SOF-02 finds lower than for stagnation blowoff.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: The fundamental limit: the lowest O2 sustaining burning of a 4-cm PMMA sphere in ISS microgravity at 101.3 kPa, slightly below 14% around 10 cm/s, from SOF-02's 35-test map.

answer.not_covered: No SoFIE-GEL extinction limit below about 101 kPa is in the documents.

answers.question: What does the burn limit SOF-02:nodate:PMMA-IN-BETWEEN:3c04b989 (PMMA, 14.6% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: An 'in-between' extinction point of SOF-02's own Fig. 8 map, test not named: the O2 recorded at extinction, about 14.6%, at about 9.2 cm/s upstream forced flow (both read from the figure); 4-cm PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity, 101.3 kPa (1 ± 0.05 atm).

Near 10 cm/s quenching was difficult to tell from blowoff on video, so SOF-02 plots some such points as open 'in-between' symbols. At intermediate flows it found the boundary by O2 depletion, O2 and flow read at the duct entrance at the extinction instant (±0.25%).

SOF-02 places the in-between points at the bottom of the boundary as the lowest O2 that sustains burning of the sample (the fundamental limit), slightly below 14% O2 around 10 cm/s, which it calls considerably lower than conventional-table normal-gravity PMMA LOI and upward values.

At about the same flow, about 9.2 cm/s, the figure has another in-between point at about 13.8% O2 labelled qc 0.51 W/cm2; the figure's mark for this limit is labelled 0.44 W/cm2. qc is the flame's conductive heat loss into the sphere at extinction.

inferred.text: Of these two Fig. 8 points, the one with the larger qc label went out at the lower O2, against SOF-02's general trend, which the paper states holds with a few exceptions; the two labels differ by less than the 20% by which SOF-02 says qc may be uncertain.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

answers.question: Why did test SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-BLACK-D2.0CM-7CMS:130d1c3b (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22% O2) burn?

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between black anodized aluminum baffles 2.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned, spreading steadily at about 0.83 mm/s (read from a figure).
Below 4.0 cm spacing the spread rate fell as the baffles closed in (7 cm/s series); the authors attribute this to oxygen starvation and conductive heat loss to the baffles.

With black baffles 1.0 cm apart, at the same about 22% O2 and 7 cm/s concurrent flow, no flame spread: one passage says it went out once the ignition energy was removed, another that ignition was not achieved.

At 2.0 cm, the smallest spacing at which a flame spread (7 cm/s series), transparent baffles gave a slightly higher spread rate than the aluminum ones; the authors read this as conductive heat loss to the close baffles, aluminum being expected to draw more heat.

inferred.text: This test's 2.0 cm spacing lies just above the quench limit that Fig. 7 draws at about 1.2 to 1.5 cm (read from a figure), and its spread rate is the lowest of its baffle type in the 7 cm/s series.

other_side.note: at 1.0 cm spacing, same baffle type and flow, no flame spread

lead.text: At 7 cm/s this test burned with baffles 2.0 cm apart, while at 1.0 cm none spread; the authors link slower close-spaced spread to oxygen starvation and baffle heat loss.

answer.not_covered: The paper tested this set-up only at the ISS ambient, about 22% O2 and 101.3 kPa.

answers.question: Why did test SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-BLACK-D3.0CM-7CMS:8ade6d04 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22% O2) burn?

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between black anodized aluminum baffles 3.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned, spreading steadily at about 1.68 mm/s (read from a figure; the figure's three 3.0 cm marks overlap).

At 3.0 cm spacing the three baffle types gave almost identical spread rates (7 cm/s series); the authors take this to suggest that at such confinement burning is limited by the oxygen supplied to the gap between the baffles.

Below 4.0 cm spacing the spread rate fell as the baffles closed in (7 cm/s series), faster than the linear trend Li et al. predicted; the authors attribute this to oxygen starvation and conductive heat loss to the baffles, adding that some flow may have been diverted outside the baffles, lowering the flow between them, especially when close.

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between black anodized aluminum baffles 5.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 5 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned until the sample was consumed, Fig. 5 printing flame-tip and flame-base spread of 1.67 mm/s.

After the igniter went off and a short growth period, the flame settled at a limiting length (1.93 cm printed in Fig. 5) and steady spread; below 15 cm/s most tests reached such a steady state, all tested spacings per the abstract.

Near the end the flame tip reached the open downstream end, accelerated and merged with the flame of the other face, then the sample was consumed and the flame quenched; the authors suspect higher flow speed, extra oxygen and reduced heat loss where the baffles end contributed to the tip acceleration.

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric without baffles, between the black duct wall and a polycarbonate window, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned, spreading steadily at about 1.2 mm/s (read from a figure).

answers.question: What does the burn limit SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-QUENCHLIMIT-7CMS:7f052b21 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Quenching limit, the baffle spacing below which SIBAL flames failed to spread, drawn in Fig. 7 at about 1.2 cm in one panel and about 1.5 cm in the other (read from the figure; ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow).
Tests at the same conditions on either side of it: with baffles 1.0 cm apart no flame spread, while at 2.0 cm, the smallest spacing at which a flame spread, all three baffle types gave steady spread.

It is the paper's own measurement, with hot-wire ignition at the leading edge kept on until a flame was established; its conclusions state that for all tested flows and baffle types a quenching spacing exists below which the flame failed to spread. Fig. 7 draws one line for all baffle types.

The abstract states that for every baffle type a spacing that is too small (about 1 cm) leaves the flame unignited or extinguished before the sample end; the authors attribute this to reduced oxygen supply to the flame zone and heat loss to the baffles.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: A quenching limit: the baffle spacing below which SIBAL fabric flames failed to spread in ISS microgravity at 7 cm/s, placed between tests at 1.0 cm and 2.0 cm.

answer.not_covered: The paper reports no test between 1.0 and 2.0 cm spacing and does not say how the line's position was set.

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between polished aluminum (reflective) baffles 1.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow (team's reading); the paper says ignition was not achieved at 1.0 cm for any baffle type.

For black baffles 1.0 cm apart at 7 cm/s, another passage says the flame went out right after the ignition energy was removed and never spread past the ignition wire (burn length under 0.8 cm), so the paper's two accounts of the 1.0 cm tests differ.

inferred.text: This test's 1.0 cm spacing lies below the quench limit that Fig. 7 draws at about 1.2 to 1.5 cm (read from a figure).

other_side.note: the same baffle type 2.0 cm apart, same flow, burned

answers.question: Why did test SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-REFLECTIVE-D3.0CM-7CMS:fd5d4cb6 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22% O2) burn?

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between polished aluminum (reflective) baffles 3.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned, spreading steadily at about 1.67 mm/s (read from a figure; the figure hides this test's mark behind the others).

At 3.0 cm spacing the three baffle types gave almost identical spread rates (7 cm/s series); the authors take this to suggest that at such confinement burning is limited by the oxygen supplied to the gap between the baffles.

Below 4.0 cm spacing the spread rate fell as the baffles closed in (7 cm/s series), faster than the linear trend Li et al. predicted; the authors attribute this to oxygen starvation and conductive heat loss to the baffles, adding that some flow may have been diverted outside the baffles, lowering the flow between them, especially when close.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: At 7 cm/s this test spread steadily with baffles 3.0 cm apart, where the three baffle types gave almost identical rates; the authors suggest the gap's oxygen supply limits burning.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1403B (PMMA, 19.9% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1403B: a 4-cm PMMA sphere in forced flow in ISS microgravity (CIR), near 101.3 kPa, hot-wire ignited. The flame quenched at 19.9% O2 and 0.84 cm/s in Table 2, 0.85 cm/s in the text, with qc 0.5 W/cm2 after 384 s from ignitor on.

SOF-02 lists this test among its quenching extinctions, which the authors attribute to excessive flame heat loss. They find that less flame heat loss into the sphere (smaller qc, more sub-surface heating) lowers the quench velocity.
Of the three Fig. 6 tests near 20% O2 (1407A, 1407B, 1403B), 1403B had the smallest qc and longest heat-up, and quenched at the lowest flow.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1403C (PMMA, 14.4% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1403C: a 4-cm PMMA sphere in ISS microgravity (CIR), hot-wire ignited at 21 cm/s, 17.74% O2 and 103.5 kPa. At 317.04 s, at 73.3 cm/s and 14.39% O2, the flame blew off locally at the stagnation point; total blowoff followed at 330 s.

SOF-02's Example #2, blowoff by flow increase: inside the duct the flow was raised quickly in steps to 75 cm/s between 250 and 290 s. O2 also depleted, but the flow changed far faster, so SOF-02 treats the flow change as the dominant cause.

After the stagnation hole opened, the flame front retreated and held in the near wake for 15 s while O2 fell from 14.39% to 13.89%. SOF-02 says wake blowoff can follow after a long delay because the flame anchors in the slower, lower-strain wake.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1403C (PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity) blew off at the stagnation point at 73.3 cm/s and 14.39% O2 after a flow increase, which SOF-02 treats as the dominant cause.

answer.not_covered: Flow and O2 at the total blowoff (330 s) are not stated separately.
